title: A cube bias across no split, split-N and split-K
surface: matmul(dst, a, b, m=, n=, k=, splitn=, splitk=, bias=) with the bias as a contiguous L1 row; gm_to_l1_pad staging that row; Position.L1 and Position.L0C tensors in a kernel(mode="cube") launch
study_for: The three staging modes are `matmul` parameters, not three kernels. `splitn=32` and `splitk=16` change how the same call partitions work inside one core, and the body around them is identical. Reading the three cases together is reading what those two keywords do.

Where the bias belongs in a split-K accumulation: on the init tile, once. The K dimension is accumulated in two passes here, and a bias added on both of them doubles exactly -- which is why the bias values are exact in FP32 and the comparison is bitwise. With a tolerance, or with a bias of zero, that failure would be invisible.

Each property of the bias row buys one detectable mistake, and `check_domain` asserts all three. Non-zero catches a bias never applied -- except in column 31, where `(arange(64) - 31) / 4` crosses zero and that one column can detect nothing; the assertion allows exactly one such column and refuses a second. Non-uniform -- `(arange(64) - 31) / 4`, sixty-four distinct values -- catches a split-N half that took the wrong slice of the row. Multiples of a quarter keep every value exact in FP32 so the comparison can be over bits.

The bias is a contiguous L1 row, moved with `gm_to_l1_pad`, and not ND2NZ-fractalized like the operands. That asymmetry in how the three L1 tensors are staged is part of the interface rather than an implementation detail of this example.

The reference does not know which split ran. It is one matmul plus one bias addition, so the three cases are three independent paths being held to a single statement of what the answer is -- rather than three references that could each drift toward their own kernel.
do_not_copy_when: You are looking for FP32 or HF32 accuracy behaviour. The inputs are small integers in [-3, 3] and the bias is a multiple of a quarter, chosen so that everything is exact. Nothing here generalises to accumulation error on real data.

Your bias is per-row rather than per-column. This is a [1, N] row broadcast down the output's rows -- the usual shape for a matmul bias. A per-row bias is a different broadcast and a different staging.

You are writing the split loops yourself. `splitn` and `splitk` are shortcuts; a hand-written tiling has to place the bias on its own init tile, and that is precisely the mistake the `splitk` case here exists to catch.
